The Build Order for Media and Publishing

The Build OrderPart 17

By lowob · 22 September 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 12-minute read · Revenue

Publishers can run The Build Order as written, provided the context layer is split in two. The commercial line is advertising, sponsorship, subscriptions, events and, increasingly, licensing content to AI companies. The wall is the newsroom: sales context must never reach editorial, and confidential reporting must never reach sales or an outside model. The pressure to build is real. Publishers surveyed by the Reuters Institute in early 2026 expect search referrals to fall by more than 40% over three years, and Chartbeat data in the same report showed organic search traffic to over 2,500 sites down 33% in a year. Pew Research found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% without one. Meanwhile the EU AI Act's transparency rules, in force since 2 August 2026, make attributable editorial responsibility the condition for publishing AI-assisted text without a label.

This is the third industry edition of The Build Order. In The RFP nobody can answer yet we said the order holds in media and publishing, with one qualification: sales context must be walled off from editorial. In The same build in four industries a composite regional publisher, funded mainly by advertising, built exactly that firewall. This piece generalises the case to publishers of every shape (consumer, specialist and business-to-business) at a moment when the economics of the sector are moving under them.

Where the commercial line sits

A publisher's commercial line has more strands than most. Each produces decisions that are frequent, similar and graded within a renewal cycle, which is the test set out in Where judgment arrives first.

LensWhat it looks like in media and publishing
Commercial lineAd and sponsorship sales, subscription pricing and retention, events, content licensing
StoreCRM, ad server and order management, subscription platform, event registration
Outcome lag30 to 90 days for retention offers; a renewal cycle for sponsors; a year or more for licensing
Who defends the decisionCommercial director, head of audience, publisher or managing director
Main rulesAdvertising disclosure rules such as the FTC's native advertising guidance; EU AI Act Article 50; press codes
The wallEditorial: drafts, sources, unpublished reporting and editorial decisions
Gateway that bitesGateway 1: brand safety and disclosure

Advertising and sponsorship. Which advertisers to pursue, when to grant a rate exception, and how to handle under-delivery through make-goods and credits. Part 10 covered this ground.

Subscriptions. Which retention offer to make to a subscriber who tries to cancel, at what discount and for how long. These decisions are made hundreds or thousands of times a month, and the outcome (still paying at 30 or 90 days, at what price) arrives quickly.

Events. Which sponsors to place at which tier, and what to discount to fill a programme.

Licensing. Whether to license an archive or a live feed to an AI developer, on what terms and for how long. This class did not exist at scale a few years ago. It is infrequent, but each decision is large and its terms shape every later one.

What the evidence says

The Reuters Institute's Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026, based on a survey of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries, found publishers expect search referrals to fall by more than 40% over three years. Chartbeat data cited in the report showed organic search traffic to more than 2,500 sites down 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and 38% in the US. The report notes it is unclear how much of that is due to AI summaries. Confidence in journalism's prospects stood at 38%. Subscriptions and membership were the leading revenue focus, cited by 76%. On licensing, 20% expected significant revenue from AI deals, 49% a minor contribution and 20% none.

Pew Research Center's browsing study of 900 US adults in March 2025 shows the mechanism at the level of individual searches. An AI summary appeared on 18% of the Google searches tracked. Where one appeared, users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits, against 15% where none appeared, and clicked a link inside the summary on 1%.

The advertising side is moving too. IAB Europe's 2026 report on AI in digital advertising found 86% of respondents reporting widespread AI use in marketing, and 58% expecting agentic ad buying to reach operational use or scale within a year. Advertising-specific AI guidance was less common than general governance. For publishers this means buyers' agents will increasingly meet sellers' systems, and whatever the publisher's agents say about audience and delivery needs to be right.

The direction is clear even where the numbers are uncertain. Referred traffic is a less reliable base. Revenue that depends on a direct relationship (subscriptions, events, sponsorship and licensing) matters more, and each of those runs on commercial decisions a publisher can record. Our piece What investors fund in media now covers the strategic side. This piece is about the build.

The build order, stage by stage

StageWhat it means in media and publishingMain risk
Gateway 0Owner on the commercial side, suite, CRM, and an editorial standards lead as data-access approver for anything near the newsroomA single owner for both commercial and editorial AI
ToolingSeats for sales, sponsorship, audience and events teams; editorial tooling bought and governed separatelyOne shared assistant across the building
ContextCommercial layer: CRM, order management, delivery reports, subscription data, rate cards. Editorial layer: separateRetrieval that crosses the firewall
RecordRetention offers, rate exceptions and make-goods, then licensing termsRecording offers without recording the outcome
ReasoningA first agent that drafts renewal and sponsor briefs from delivery data into a queueMisstated audience or delivery figures
Gateway 1Named approval for anything sent to a client; stricter rules for sponsored contentUnlabelled or ambiguously labelled commercial content
Gateway 2Value of each exception or offer; retained revenue written backDiscounts that retain subscribers at a loss
Gateway 3Extension to ad operations, finance and audience development, never into editorialTreating editorial as just another department

Gateway 0. The owner sits on the commercial side. Add a data-access approver from editorial standards who must sign off any source that sits near the newsroom: shared drives, content management systems, analytics that show story-level performance. Part 3, Gateway 0, sets out the standing decisions.

Tooling. Seats go to the commercial teams. If the newsroom uses AI tools, it buys and governs them on its own terms. Two teams sharing one assistant with one memory is the most common way the firewall fails.

Context. The commercial context layer connects the CRM, order management, campaign delivery reports, rate cards, the subscription platform and event registrations. Part 5, The context layer, followed through one account, explains how to connect in order of usefulness. The next section explains what stays out.

Record. Start with subscription retention offers if the publisher has a meaningful subscription base. Each record holds the offer, the reason (price sensitivity, content fit, payment failure), the owner or rule that made it, the value at stake and a check at 30 and 90 days. Then rate exceptions and make-goods. Then licensing: record the first AI licensing deal with its terms, the alternatives considered and what the publisher expected it to be worth, because every later negotiation will be compared with it.

Reasoning. The first agent drafts renewal briefs and sponsor proposals from delivery data, into a queue for a person to check. It is a good first job because every figure in a renewal brief can be checked against a delivery report, so errors are caught before a client sees them.

The firewall: two context layers that never meet

The wall in media runs in both directions.

Commercial context must not reach editorial. An assistant that can see an advertiser's renewal thread and an editor's draft side by side breaches editorial independence, whatever the file permissions allow. A brand that is about to renew should not appear as a suggestion in an editor's research. Story-level performance data shared with sales is a judgment call each publisher makes under its own standards; it should be made once, by the data-access approver, and recorded.

Editorial material must not reach sales or outside models. Unpublished reporting, source identities, embargoed material and editorial decision notes stay inside the editorial system. They never enter the commercial layer, and they never go to an outside model under terms that allow training or human review by the vendor.

Licensing sits on the line. A licensing deal is a commercial decision about editorial assets. The record of the deal belongs in the commercial layer. The content licensed is defined by editorial, and the commercial agent never has access to the archive itself, only to the terms.

The firewall is not a permission setting. It is two context layers, each with its own owner, that never share a memory.

Gateway 1: disclosure and brand safety

Gateway 1, nothing sends without a person, is stricter in media for two reasons.

Native and sponsored content must be identifiable. The FTC's guidance on native advertising says an ad should not suggest it is anything other than an ad. Terms such as "Ad", "Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" are likely to be understood; "Promoted" is described as ambiguous. Disclosures should sit in front of or above the headline and carry over when content is republished. An agent drafting sponsored content must use the approved label every time, and the approver checks the label as well as the copy. Our pieces Native advertising and sponsored content and Brand safety and suitability cover the commercial practice.

AI-generated public-interest text needs a named editor or a label. Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act, applicable since 2 August 2026, requires disclosure when AI-generated or AI-manipulated text is published to inform the public on matters of public interest. There is an exemption where the text has undergone human review and someone holds editorial responsibility. The European Commission's draft guidelines of May 2026, as summarised by Greenberg Traurig, read that exemption narrowly: a person with relevant expertise must review the substance, and an identifiable person or organisation with authority to approve, amend or reject the text must be publicly accountable for it. Spelling and grammar checks do not count. For a publisher this has a practical effect. Commercial content drafted with AI, such as a sponsored explainer, needs the same quality of attributable sign-off as editorial copy, or it needs a label.

The Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, left most Article 50 obligations on their original date and gave generative AI systems already on the market until 2 December 2026 to meet the machine-readable marking requirement, according to White & Case. Publishers should treat 2 August 2026 as the date their own disclosure duties began.

Gateways 2 and 3

Gateway 2. The dollar figure is straightforward for most media decisions. A retention offer has a cost (the discount multiplied by its duration) and a value (revenue retained beyond the offer period). A rate exception has a value at stake and a renewal outcome. Write the outcome back to each decision. A common early finding is that a generous retention offer keeps subscribers who cancel as soon as it expires, which the record shows at the 90-day check.

Gateway 3. The record extends to ad operations, finance and audience development. It does not extend into editorial. If the newsroom builds its own brain, it is a separate build with its own owner, its own record and its own gateways.

Illustrative example: a specialist publisher records its retention offers
Decision
Record every subscription retention offer and every sponsorship rate exception, with reason, value at stake and checks at 30 and 90 days, before connecting any agent.
Reason and owner
Search referrals had fallen and subscriptions and events had become the main revenue lines; nobody knew which retention offers kept subscribers after the discount ended. Owned by the commercial director, with the editor-in-chief's deputy as data-access approver.
What changed
The first agent drafts sponsor renewal briefs from delivery data into a review queue and never reads the editorial content system. After one quarter, the 90-day checks showed the deepest discount retained no more subscribers beyond its term than a smaller one, and the publisher withdrew it.

Illustrative: a composite of a business-to-business specialist publisher of around 120 people, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Split the context layer. Commercial and editorial each get their own wiring, owner and memory.
  • Start where outcomes arrive fastest. Retention offers are graded in weeks; record them first.
  • Record the first licensing deal properly. Every later negotiation will be measured against it.
  • Label every time. Sponsored content needs an approved label, and AI-assisted public-interest text needs a named editor or a disclosure.
  • Never extend Gateway 3 into the newsroom. An editorial brain is a separate build.
Gateway card

Before a publisher connects its first agent

  • Separate owners for commercial and editorial AI, and an editorial data-access approver
  • A commercial context layer that excludes the content management system, drafts and source material
  • Vendor terms checked so editorial material never trains an outside model
  • Retention offers and rate exceptions recorded with value at stake and 30- and 90-day checks
  • Approved disclosure labels built into every sponsored-content draft
  • A named, accountable approver for any AI-assisted text published to the public

Common questions

How should publishers use AI without compromising editorial independence?

Build two context layers that never meet: one for commercial teams (CRM, delivery, subscriptions) and one for the newsroom, with separate owners and tools. Commercial agents should never read editorial drafts or sources, and editorial tools should never see advertiser threads.

Does the EU AI Act require publishers to label AI-generated articles?

Article 50(4), applicable from 2 August 2026, requires disclosure of AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has had human review and someone holds editorial responsibility. The Commission's draft guidelines read that exemption narrowly.

How much traffic are publishers losing to AI search?

Chartbeat data in the Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report showed organic search traffic to over 2,500 sites down 33% globally in the year to November 2025, and publishers expect a further fall of more than 40% over three years. How much is due to AI summaries is unclear.

What is the best first AI agent for a media company's sales team?

A clerk that drafts sponsor renewal briefs and proposals from delivery data into a review queue. Staff can check every figure against delivery reports, which builds trust before anything more ambitious.
